say.text: Welcome. Today's big question: how can we know about people who never wrote a word? We'll learn what prehistory means, the main kinds of evidence, and why dates sometimes change.

show.text: How we know: reading the deep past without writing

say.text: Let's start with the word itself. Prehistory means the time before there were written records.

show.text: Prehistory = the time before written records

ask.right: The time before there were written records
wrong: The time before the Earth formed
The time before humans could talk
The time before humans used fire
ask.why: Pre means before. History, in this sense, is the time with written records. Prehistory is the time before them.

say.text: So there are no letters, no diaries, no names. For prehistory, the only sources are material and environmental: things people left behind, and the world around them.

show.text:
What prehistory has instead of writing:
- things people made
- things people left behind
- the natural world around them

say.text: Where does prehistory end? Not on one date. It ends where written records begin, and that happens at different times in different places.

show.text: Prehistory ends when writing begins, place by place

ask.q: Does prehistory end on the same date everywhere in the world?
ask.right: No. It ends when written records begin in each place.
wrong: Yes, it ended on one date for the whole world
Yes, it ended when the Ice Age ended
No, it has never ended anywhere
ask.why: Prehistory is defined by missing writing, and writing arrived at different times in different places.

say.text: It's a very long story. One source says the earliest technology began about 2.5 million years ago. The Old Stone Age covers roughly 99% of technological prehistory.

show.text: about 2.5 million years since the earliest technology

say.text: So what do we use instead of writing? Four main kinds of evidence: bones, tools, hearths and DNA. Then we need a way to date them. We'll take them one at a time.

show.text:
Our evidence kit:
1. Bones and teeth
2. Tools
3. Hearths (old fires)
4. Ancient DNA
+ Dating methods

say.text: First, bones. A fossil is a bone, tooth or trace of ancient life that survived in the ground. Very old fossils are rare. Those over 3.5 million years old are extremely rare.

show.text: 1,550 bone pieces from at least 15 individuals, found in one South African cave

ask.right: A bone, tooth or trace of ancient life that has survived in the ground
wrong: A written note from long ago
A tool made from stone
A painting on a cave wall
ask.why: Fossils are the physical remains or traces of ancient living things. They are one of our main clues.

say.text: Second, tools. Stone tools are what mark the Old Stone Age. A shaped stone tells us that someone chose it, made it and used it.

show.text: A teardrop-shaped flint handaxe, chipped on both sides to make a sharp edge

say.text: Third, hearths, which are the traces of old fires. At Gesher Benot Ya'aqov in Israel, scorched toolmaking debris lay near burned seeds and wood. Those mark early hearths.

show.text: Dark, scorched flint flakes lying beside charred seeds and burned wood in an excavation trench

say.text: Notice this site has two dates. One is when people used it, about 790,000 years ago. The other is when archaeologists found it, in the early 1930s. We'll give both for every site.

show.text:
Gesher Benot Ya'aqov, Israel
Used: about 790,000 years ago | Found: early 1930s

ask.q: When did archaeologists find Gesher Benot Ya'aqov?
wrong: About 790,000 years ago
In the year 1790
Nobody has found it yet
ask.why: 790,000 years ago is when people used the site. The early 1930s is when archaeologists found it. They are two different events.

say.text: Fourth, ancient DNA. DNA is the instruction code inside living cells. In 2010, scientists recovered DNA from a finger bone found in Denisova Cave in Siberia. It showed a group of humans who were neither modern humans nor Neanderthals: the Denisovans.

show.text: A tiny fossil finger bone resting in a gloved hand under bright lab light

ask.q: What did the DNA from the Denisova Cave finger bone show?
ask.right: A previously unknown group of early humans, now called Denisovans
wrong: That the bone belonged to a modern person
That the bone was a Neanderthal
That the bone was from a chimpanzee
ask.why: The DNA matched neither modern humans nor Neanderthals. It was the first time a new human group was identified from ancient DNA.

say.text: DNA can also show family links. Fossils from Sima de los Huesos in Spain are 430,000 years old. Their DNA showed they were early Neanderthals. Early DNA work did struggle with contamination, though.

show.text: DNA: family links, and a contamination risk

say.text: Now: how old is any of this? Fossils often lie between two layers of volcanic ash. Date the layer above and the layer below, and the object sits in between.

show.text: A cliff face in stripes: a pale ash layer on top, a bone in the middle, another ash layer below

say.text: Another way is radiocarbon dating. All living things take in carbon, including a rare radioactive kind called carbon-14. When a plant or animal dies, the carbon-14 slowly decays. Start with 8 dots of carbon-14.

show.text: Alive: 8 dots of carbon-14

say.text: The time for half of it to decay is called a half-life. For carbon-14 that is about 5,730 years. After one half-life, half is left: 4 dots.

show.text: After about 5,730 years: 4 dots left

say.text: After two half-lives, a quarter is left: 2 dots. That means about 11,460 years. Scientists measure what is left and work back to the age.

show.text: After about 11,460 years: 2 dots left

ask.q: A piece of charcoal has a quarter of its original carbon-14. About how old is it?
wrong: About 5,730 years
About 22,920 years
About 50,000 years
ask.why: A quarter left means two half-lives, and two times 5,730 is about 11,460 years.

say.text: Every method has limits. Limit one: radiocarbon only works on things that were once alive, like wood, bone, shell, charcoal and seeds. It cannot date a stone tool directly.

show.text: Can be dated: charcoal, bone, seeds, wood | Cannot be dated: stone tools, pottery

say.text: Limit two: age. Radiocarbon effectively stops at about 50,000 years. After that, too little carbon-14 is left to measure. Some sources say 55,000 or 60,000, which we'll come back to.

show.text: about 50,000 years: radiocarbon's limit

ask.q: Could radiocarbon dating be used on a bone that is one million years old?
ask.right: No. It is far too old, and too little carbon-14 would be left.
wrong: Yes, radiocarbon works on any age
Yes, but only if the bone is very large
No, because bones were never alive
ask.why: The limit is around 50,000 years. Bones were once alive, so material isn't the problem here. The age is.

say.text: Limit three: contamination. Say a 50,000-year-old sample picks up just 1% modern carbon from glue or soil. It would be dated to around 35,000 years. So samples are cleaned very carefully.

show.text: 1% modern carbon can make 50,000 look like about 35,000

say.text: One more step. Raw results are corrected using a calibration curve, built from things of known age such as tree rings. In 2008 that curve reached only 26,000 years. Now it reaches about 55,000, though the oldest part is less certain.

show.text:
2008: calibration reaches about 26,000 years
Now: about 55,000 years, the oldest part less certain

say.text: Here are some of our example finds by age. Radiocarbon stops near 50,000 years. Look at the bars and see which ones fall far beyond it.

show.text: Ages of example finds (years ago)

ask.q: Which of these is too old for radiocarbon to date directly?
ask.right: The hearths at Gesher Benot Ya'aqov, about 790,000 years old
wrong: Göbekli Tepe, about 11,500 years old
A seed that is 5,000 years old
A bone that is 30,000 years old
ask.why: Radiocarbon reaches only about 50,000 years. The 790,000-year-old hearths are far beyond that. The other items are all within range.

say.text: For older things, scientists use other clocks. Potassium-argon dating works on volcanic rock and ash, from about 100,000 years to billions. It dates the layers, so the fossil gets a date between them.

show.text: A scientist chipping a sample from a pale volcanic ash layer in a gorge wall, a fossil site just above it

ask.q: A 1.8-million-year-old fossil lies between two volcanic ash layers. Which clock suits it?
ask.right: Potassium-argon (or argon-argon) dating of the ash layers
wrong: Radiocarbon dating of the fossil
Counting tree rings
Reading a written record
ask.why: Volcanic ash can be dated with potassium-argon methods, and the fossil sits between the dated layers. Radiocarbon is far too short-range here.

say.text: Now the next big idea: evidence is patchy. Very old fossils are extremely rare, and the people had no writing. One researcher put it simply: words do not fossilise.

show.text: 'words do not fossilise'

say.text: Dates can be wrong, and then they get fixed. The KBS Tuff is an ash layer in East Africa. One early study gave about 2.6 million years. Other evidence disagreed, and several methods later supported about 1.87 million.

show.text:
Early estimate: about 2.61 million years
Later, several methods agree: about 1.87 million years

say.text: Here's a famous puzzle. Homo naledi bones were found in a South African cave in 2013, and the species was named in 2015. At first nobody knew how old they were.

show.text: Homo naledi: found 2013, named 2015, age unknown

say.text: The bones looked primitive, so many experts guessed over 1.5 million years old. But the bones seemed barely fossilised. In 2017, dating of teeth and cave rock gave 236,000 to 335,000 years.

show.text:
Dinaledi Chamber, South Africa
Bones laid down: 236,000 to 335,000 years ago | Found: 2013

ask.q: Why was the age of Homo naledi such a surprise?
ask.right: Its bones looked very old and primitive, but dating showed it lived much more recently
wrong: It turned out to be a modern human
The bones were found to be fake
Dating showed it was over two million years old
ask.why: Looks alone suggested a very old species. Direct dating placed it between 236,000 and 335,000 years ago. Looks can mislead, so dating matters.

say.text: Better tools also change dates. A hunting scene at Leang Bulu' Sipong 4 in Sulawesi was first dated to at least 43,900 years; a new laser method pushed it to at least 48,000. The same method dated a scene at nearby Leang Karampuang to at least 51,200.

show.text:
Leang Karampuang, Indonesia
Painted: at least 51,200 years ago | Found: 2017

say.text: Sometimes the evidence stays the same and the reading changes. Göbekli Tepe in Turkey was built about 9,500 BCE. A 1960s survey saw worked stones and took them for a later cemetery.

show.text:
Göbekli Tepe, Turkey
Built: about 9500 BCE (roughly 11,500 years ago) | Rediscovered: 1994; digging began 1995

ask.q: Why is 1994 called a 'rediscovery' of Göbekli Tepe?
ask.right: Archaeologists had noted the stones earlier, but only in 1994 did Klaus Schmidt recognise how important the site was
wrong: The site was built in 1994
The site had been lost under the sea
The first survey found writing there
ask.why: The site was recorded in the 1960s and misread. In 1994 Klaus Schmidt identified its T-shaped pillars, and excavation began in 1995.

say.text: So why do stories get revised? Three main reasons: new finds, better methods, and new readings of old evidence. One find showed our species is about 100,000 years older than first thought.

show.text:
Why the story changes:
- new finds
- better dating methods
- new readings of old evidence

ask.q: Which best explains why scientists revise dates and stories?
ask.right: New finds and better methods give new evidence, and the story is updated to fit it
wrong: Scientists change their minds for fun
The old dates were just guesses with no science
Dates are decided by a vote
ask.why: Revision is how science works. Evidence is tested, and when new finds or methods give better answers, the story is updated.

say.text: Let's see where our example sites are, from South Africa to Israel, Spain, England, Turkey and Indonesia. All of them are far apart and far apart in time.

show.text: A world map with six marked sites: Rising Star Cave (South Africa), Gesher Benot Ya'aqov (Israel), Sima de los Huesos (Spain), Barnham (England), Göbekli Tepe (Turkey), Leang Karampuang (Indonesia)

say.text: Here's the whole course in one line, oldest first. We'll fill in each part over the next nine classes. Some dates are firm, and some are still argued over.

show.text:
8-6 million years ago: human and chimpanzee lines split
about 2.5 million years ago: earliest stone technology (one source)
2.6 million to 11,700 years ago: the Ice Age (Pleistocene)
430,000 years ago: earliest Neanderthals, shown by DNA
about 400,000 years ago: deliberate fire-making at Barnham, England
about 300,000 years ago: earliest Homo sapiens remains
about 70,000 years ago: our ancestors spread from Africa
at least 51,200 years ago: oldest narrative cave painting
about 11,500 years ago: Göbekli Tepe built
about 10,000 years ago: farming begins

ask.q: Which of these is the OLDEST?
ask.right: The first stone tools, about 2.5 million years ago
wrong: The earliest Homo sapiens remains, about 300,000 years ago
The Sulawesi narrative painting, at least 51,200 years ago
Göbekli Tepe, about 11,500 years ago
ask.why: Stone tools go back about 2.5 million years in the source we used, far older than the other three.

say.text: Let's recap. Prehistory is the time before writing. We read it from bones, tools, hearths and DNA, and date them with clocks that each have limits. Dates change when new evidence arrives. Next class: walking upright.

show.text:
Today you learned:
- Prehistory = before written records
- Evidence: bones, tools, hearths, DNA
- Dating clocks, each with a limit
- Patchy evidence and new finds change the story
Next: Class 2, Walking upright

frame_of_reference.elsewhere: Denisovans were living in Asia (the Denisova finger bone is 76,000 to 52,000 years old), and Neanderthals were making fire at a site in France around 50,000 years ago.
The last Ice Age was ending about 11,700 years ago, and farming began about 10,000 years ago.
In Spain, early Neanderthals lived at Sima de los Huesos about 430,000 years ago, and by then Neanderthal and Denisovan lines had already split.

other_side.claim: 'Prehistory' is a useful label for the time before writing.
other_side.other_view: The word came from an early view that without writing there is no history. Some scholars say ancient people should not be treated as a separate 'prehistoric' world, because learning about them matters to living communities today.

other_side.claim: Göbekli Tepe was mainly a temple or ritual site.
other_side.other_view: Its first 20 years of study saw it as mainly ritual. Findings published in 2019 suggest a settlement with domestic structures, and specialists still debate whether 'temple' is the right word.

other_side.claim: The oldest firm evidence of deliberate fire-making is about 400,000 years old (Barnham, England).
other_side.other_view: Claims for the earliest use of fire run back as far as 2.0 million years. Some older sites, such as Koobi Fora in Kenya, cannot rule out wildfire. Fire-making and fire-using also follow different timelines.

other_side.claim: The shape of a fossil is a good guide to its age.
other_side.other_view: Many anthropologists judged from its anatomy that Homo naledi was over 1.5 million years old. Direct dating later placed it at 236,000 to 335,000 years.
Other sources give 55,000 or 60,000 years, and special preparation can sometimes handle older samples. Uncertainty grows with age, and calibration beyond about 50,000 years is still tentative.
